title: Lower cardinality estimate for substring/LIKE table filters
hypothesis: In q09 the scan on the filtered dimension table (contains(name,'word'), from LIKE '%word%') gets DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY 0.2 in RelationStatisticsHelper::ExtractGetStats. The real selectivity is about 5% (est 400K rows, actual 109K). That inflates every estimate above it: fact⋈dim is estimated at 12M (actual 3.27M) and the top 2-key join at 47.9M (actual 3.27M). As a result BuildProbeSideOptimizer builds hash tables on the big sides: 15M orders (HASH_JOIN 2.49s cumulative) and 8M partsupp⋈supplier⋈nation (2.29s), each probed with only 3.27M rows. I set disabled_optimizers='join_order,build_side_probe_side' and wrote the joins by hand so that the small intermediate is the build side of both joins: EXPLAIN ANALYZE total went from 1.40s to 0.725s on the same tool. Substring matching on free text is selective in general, and Postgres-style estimators give LIKE patterns much lower selectivity than plain range filters.
plan: In src/optimizer/join_order/relation_statistics_helper.cpp, ExtractGetStats, lines 119-155: when a non-optional table filter is an ExpressionFilter (TableFilterType::EXPRESSION_FILTER, possibly inside a ConjunctionAndFilter) whose expression is a BoundFunctionExpression named contains / like / ~~ / ilike / ~~* / regexp_matches / suffix (with a constant pattern argument), apply a lower selectivity, e.g. a new constant STRING_PATTERN_SELECTIVITY = 0.05 in relation_statistics_helper.hpp, instead of DEFAULT_SELECTIVITY. Keep the existing rule that an equality filter estimate wins (MinValue). If the expression is anything else, behaviour stays exactly as it is now. Then check the q09 EXPLAIN: the part-side estimate should be about 100K and the orders/partsupp joins should flip or be reordered. If the partsupp join still builds on the 8M side because the 2-key join estimate counts only one key, record that in the ledger as a follow-up; don't widen this diff.
expected_gain: q09: 20-45% if both big builds flip (the hand-written plan measured 1.40s down to 0.73s); about 15-20% if only the orders join flips.
generality: Any star or snowflake join where a dimension is filtered by LIKE '%x%', contains, or a suffix/regex filter: the join order and build side improve. Could get slower: queries whose substring filter is not selective (e.g. LIKE '%a%'), where a big table might now be chosen as the build side by mistake. Results stay correct because only plan choice changes.
risk: Low for correctness, since this only changes estimates. Medium for performance on unseen queries that have unselective LIKE filters. Plan changes can also shift other templates in either direction.

title: Multi-key join cardinality: use the most selective key, not one key
hypothesis: The top join in q09 (fact⋈dim) ⋈ partsupp ON partkey AND suppkey is estimated at 47.9M although the input is 12M and the composite key is unique on the build side. The estimator seems to divide only by one key's distinct count (12M*8M/2M), so the probe side looks 4x bigger than the 8M build side and the build stays on partsupp (2.29s).
plan: Look into CardinalityEstimator (src/optimizer/join_order/cardinality_estimator.cpp): how the denominator is computed when several equality edges connect the same two relation sets. Have it use the product of the key distinct counts, capped at the larger side's cardinality, or the max. Do this only after the selectivity issue lands, and only if the partsupp join still builds on the big side.
expected_gain: q09: up to about 20% more if the partsupp join flips to build on the small intermediate.
generality: Joins on composite keys (e.g. fact to bridge tables on two FKs). Could underestimate correlated multi-key joins.
risk: Medium: the estimator is used by every multi-join plan.

title: Bloom filter pushdown for multi-key hash joins on the first key
hypothesis: After E0001 the q09 plan joins lineitem to (partsupp⋈part, 436K rows) on two keys: l_partkey=p_partkey AND l_suppkey=ps_suppkey. The profile shows the lineitem TABLE_SCAN emitting 59,986,046 rows (2.74s cumulative) with only min/max dynamic filters, and the 2-key HASH_JOIN at 2.27s probing 60M rows to produce 3.27M. No bloom filter is pushed because JoinFilterPushdownInfo::CanUseBloomFilter (physical_hash_join.cpp:775) requires ht->conditions.size()==1. That check exists because the hash table's row hash combines all keys, so a probe side that hashes one column can't test it. If we build a separate bloom filter from the hash of the first key column alone (VectorOperations::Hash of that column, which is exactly what BFTableFilter::HashInternal computes on the probe side), the scan can drop about 95% of lineitem rows early. Before E0001 the BF on l_partkey cut lineitem to 3.45M rows. So the new plan plus that BF should take most of the 2.7s scan and 2.3s join time out of the query.
plan: 1) In physical_hash_join.cpp CanUseBloomFilter: allow conditions.size()>1 when the filter being pushed is for condition index 0 (pass filter_idx in, or check it in FinalizeFilters at line 899), as long as that condition is COMPARE_EQUAL. Keep the other checks (build_side_has_filter, probe>build, no perfect HT, no cast). 2) In join_hashtable.cpp: when should_build_bloom_filter is set and conditions.size()>1, JoinHashTable::Finalize (line 775) should not insert the stored combined row hashes into bloom_filter in InsertHashes. Instead, for each chunk, gather key column 0 from row_locations using data_collection->Gather(row_locations_vector, sel, count, column_id=0, key_vector, sel, nullptr) (tuple_data_collection.hpp:213; the key columns come first in the layout), run VectorOperations::Hash(key_vector, hashes, count), then bloom_filter.InsertHashes(hashes, count). The single-key path stays unchanged. 3) PushBloomFilter already uses conditions[0] for key name, type and NullValuesAreEqual(0), so it stays correct. Before the change, check that the multi-key HT row hash is not what the BF probe expects anywhere else (e.g. a probe-side BF check in JoinHashTable::Probe using bloom_filter on the combined hash). Grep join_hashtable.cpp for bloom_filter uses. If the HT itself probes the BF with combined hashes, keep that path disabled for multi-key or use a separate BloomFilter member for pushdown.
expected_gain: q09: lineitem rows into the 2-key join should drop from 60M to about 3.5M. Expect 30-50% on q09 (725ms to about 400-500ms).
generality: Any star or snowflake query that joins a large fact table to a filtered dimension or bridge on a composite key (e.g. fact ⋈ partsupp-like tables on 2 FKs, or multi-column date/key joins). SelectivityOptionalFilter switches the BF off at runtime when it doesn't filter, so non-selective first keys cost only the sampled checks plus the build-side gather and hash (small, build is the smaller side). Joins that could get slower: multi-key joins with a large build side, which pay an extra gather and hash pass at finalize.
risk: Medium. Correctness depends on the BF hash matching the probe-side hash exactly (same column type, same VectorOperations::Hash). A mismatch would wrongly drop rows, so test multi-key joins, including NULL keys, a VARCHAR first key and an external/partitioned hash join. The has_cast check must stay.

title: Software prefetch of hash-table entries and rows in hash join probe
hypothesis: In q09.m0 the largest operator is HASH_JOIN o_orderkey=l_orderkey at 1.77-1.87s cumulative. It makes 15M probes against a hash table built on 3.27M lineitem rows: the pointer table is about 8M entries (64MB) and the row data is over 100MB, both far larger than the caches. Probing ~15M rows costs about 120ns per row, which is a DRAM miss per probe. ProbeForPointersInternal (join_hashtable.cpp:188) loads entries[hash & bitmask] one row at a time with no prefetch, and row_matcher_build.Match then dereferences each row pointer, which is a second random miss. The codebase has no __builtin_prefetch anywhere. I checked whether a bloom filter on the orders side would avoid this. Disabling compressed_materialization lets the BF reach the orders scan (it then emits 2.96M rows instead of 15M), but wall time did not improve (533 vs 509 ms), because the scan cost rose by as much as the join saved. Hiding the miss latency inside the probe is the remaining lever.
plan: In src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp: (1) In ProbeForPointersInternal<USE_SALTS,HAS_SEL>, before the main loop, add a pass over hashes_dense[0..count) that issues __builtin_prefetch(&entries[hashes_dense[i] & ht.bitmask]). Guard it with #if defined(__GNUC__) || defined(__clang__) and run it only when the table is large (ht.capacity * sizeof(ht_entry_t) above a fixed constant such as 1MB, an L2-scale constant, not tied to data). With USE_SALTS each entry fits one cache line, so the main loop then hits cache. (2) In GetRowPointersInternal, after ProbeForPointers returns keys_to_compare_count and before row_matcher_build.Match, prefetch the row pointers for keys_to_compare_sel[0..keys_to_compare_count) from pointers_result_v (data_ptr_t), under the same size guard. Make no logic changes: prefetch is only a hint, so results are identical. Optionally apply the same entry prefetch in the build insert loop (InsertRowToEntry caller, ~line 584/671) only if it is trivial; otherwise leave it out.
expected_gain: q09: the orders join (~1.8s of ~6s cumulative) could drop by 30-50%, and the 2-key lineitem join (0.67s) a little. Roughly 8-15% on q09 wall time.
generality: Every hash join whose hash table exceeds the cache (large build sides: fact-to-fact joins, joins of large dimension tables, and large intermediates). Small hash tables are unaffected because of the size guard. A small regression is possible when probes are mostly sequential and cache-friendly, where the extra pass costs a loop over 2048 hashes per vector (negligible).
risk: Low. No semantic change, and the prefetch is guarded to GCC/Clang. The main risk is no measurable gain, if the hardware already overlaps the misses through out-of-order execution.

title: Hash join prefetch v2: build insert + probe, software-pipelined, LLC-sized threshold
hypothesis: Batch wall-clock timing (dbe-tool sql running 3-5 copies of a query; profile operator times are inflated about 4x by profiling) puts q09 at about 165 ms per run. Building it up one join at a time: lineitem⋈part (with BF) costs about 20 ms, partsupp⋈part about 12 ms, the 2-key lineitem⋈partsupp probe (3.27M probes, 1M-entry/8MB HT, 14MB of rows) about 30 ms, and the orders join (15M probes into a 3.27M-row build, so 8M entries = 64MB of ht_entry_t, with about 80% misses) about 50-65 ms. So about 90 of the 165 ms is hash-join build/probe, and that is bound by memory latency. The lineitem scan, although it shows 3.6s in the profile, is only about 20-30 ms of wall time. In ProbeForPointersInternal (join_hashtable.cpp:188) the salted linear-probe loop has a data-dependent `while(true)`/break on whether a slot is occupied (about 41% occupancy, so mispredictions are frequent). That stops the CPU from overlapping the DRAM misses. E0003 measured -5.7%/-4.8% with probe prefetch only, and -9.9%/-5.6% with build prefetch added, but the official run was -4.7%, just under the bar. This version differs as follows: (1) build and probe prefetch always ship together, since the build prefetch was the larger part of the gain; (2) prefetch runs a fixed distance ahead inside the loops (i+PREFETCH_DISTANCE, e.g. 16), not as a 2048-wide pre-pass, so it does not over-subscribe the line-fill buffers and gets no extra loop pass on small inputs; (3) it is gated on the HT entry array being larger than about 4MB (not 1MB), so mid-size HTs that fit in cache pay nothing; (4) it also prefetches the chained row in ScanStructure::AdvancePointers/Next when chains_longer_than_one is set.
plan:
src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp only:
(a) Add a file-local helper `static inline void PrefetchRead(const void *p)` / `PrefetchWrite` that wraps __builtin_prefetch under #if defined(__GNUC__)||defined(__clang__), and is a no-op otherwise. Add a file-local constexpr PREFETCH_DISTANCE=16 and a constexpr byte threshold of 4MB, compared against ht.capacity*sizeof(ht_entry_t).
(b) ProbeForPointersInternal: when over the threshold, at the top of iteration i prefetch entries[hashes_dense[i+D] & ht.bitmask] if i+D<count. Use template dispatch, or a bool hoisted outside the loop, so the small-HT path is unchanged.
(c) GetRowPointersInternal: before row_matcher_build.Match, prefetch the row pointers for keys_to_compare_sel (pointers_result_v data) in a short loop. This touches only `keys_to_compare_count` pointers, which is cheap.
(d) InsertHashesLoop (the build): at the top of each insert iteration, prefetch the target entry for write at distance D.
(e) ScanStructure::AdvancePointers (or wherever the chain next pointer is followed) when ht.chains_longer_than_one: prefetch the next row pointer.
No header changes and no semantic changes.
expected_gain: q09: 6-10% (E0003 already measured -5% to -10% with a cruder pass; the distance-based version plus the build prefetch should land at the upper end). Any query with a hash join whose HT exceeds the LLC should gain too.
generality: Every hash join with a large build side (more than about 250K rows): star and snowflake fact⋈dim joins, fact⋈fact joins on orderkey, TPC-H Q3/5/7/8/9/18/21-style queries. Queries with small HTs skip it because of the threshold. Nothing can return different results, since prefetch is only a hint. Worst case is a few percent of extra instructions on large-HT joins that are already cache-resident (unlikely above 4MB).
risk: Low for correctness. The risk is in measurement: the gain may again come in near the 5% noise bar. The implementer should bench q09 at least twice and report both runs.

title: Bitpacking select: decode only the selected rows' blocks for filtered scans
hypothesis: In q09 the lineitem scan applies the part BF on l_partkey (60M rows in, 3.27M out, about 5.5%) and then fetches 4 non-filter BitPacking columns: l_orderkey (DELTA_FOR), l_quantity, l_extendedprice, l_discount (all FOR). Bitpacking registers no `select` callback (bitpacking.cpp GetBitpackingFunction sets only scan/scan_partial/fetch_row/skip), so StandardColumnData::Select (standard_column_data.cpp:103) takes the ColumnData::Select fallback. That fallback decodes all 2048 values, applies FOR to all of them, and then Slices, which hands a dictionary vector to every downstream operator. Measured with 5-run batches: lineitem JOIN part (BF) with count(*) only is 21.5 ms/run. Adding sums over l_extendedprice, l_suppkey, l_orderkey, l_quantity and l_discount gives 44.5 ms/run, so the non-filter columns cost about 20 ms of q09's roughly 83 ms/run. (l_suppkey has a min/max dynamic filter, so it is decoded as a filter column either way.) A select that unpacks only the 32-value algorithm blocks that contain a selected row, writes only the selected values into a compact flat vector, and skips the Slice should remove a large part of that cost.
plan: In src/storage/compression/bitpacking.cpp add `template <class T, class T_S = MakeSigned<T>::type, class T_U = ...> void BitpackingSelect(ColumnSegment &segment, ColumnScanState &state, idx_t vector_count, Vector &result, const SelectionVector &sel, idx_t sel_count)`, using the signature of RLESelect (rle.cpp:427) and DictFSSTSelect, and register it in GetBitpackingFunction with `bitpacking.select = BitpackingSelect<T>;`. Implementation: mirror the loop in BitpackingScanPartial (bitpacking.cpp:775), walking the vector_count positions through metadata groups (LoadNextGroup when current_group_offset == BITPACKING_METADATA_GROUP_SIZE) and 32-value algorithm groups, while keeping a cursor into sel. The sel indices are ascending; throw an InternalException if they are not, as RLE does. Per mode: CONSTANT writes current_constant for the selected indices in range. CONSTANT_DELTA writes constant*offset + FOR for the selected indices. FOR: if no selected index falls in this 32-block, only advance current_group_offset (no unpack); otherwise UnPackBlock into scan_state.decompression_buffer and write buffer[off]+FOR for each selected index in the block. DELTA_FOR: always unpack, ApplyFrameOfReference plus DeltaDecode into the decompression buffer (the delta chain needs every value), update current_delta_offset, and copy out the selected values. At the end the scan state must sit exactly vector_count positions further on, the same as after BitpackingScan. Set the result to FLAT_VECTOR with result_data[i] for i < sel_count. Validity is handled separately in StandardColumnData::Select (it already requires validity_has_select), so do not touch it. Test with dbe-tool sql: filtered scans comparing sum/min/max of FOR, DELTA_FOR and constant columns (e.g. sorted keys, low-cardinality ints, dates, decimals) against the same query with the filter wrapped so it is not pushed down. Use selectivities of 0.1%, 5%, 50% and 99%, and also run a query on a column that contains NULLs.
expected_gain: q09: about 5-12% (the measured 20 ms of non-filter column decode at 5.5% selectivity; about 16% of FOR blocks are skipped entirely, and the full-vector FOR pass, the 2048-wide writes and the dictionary Slice all go away).
generality: Any scan of a BitPacking integer, date or decimal column (the default for most integer data) that has a selective pushed filter or a dynamic join filter (BF or min/max) on another column. At 1% selectivity about 72% of the blocks are skipped. This is common in star-schema fact scans. Downstream operators also get flat vectors instead of dictionary slices. Possible slowdown: near-100% selectivity adds a little per-index bookkeeping compared with a straight decode. The implementer may fall back to scan+copy when sel_count > about 0.75*vector_count.
risk: Medium-low. It is an isolated new callback, but scan-state advancement must match Scan exactly. An off-by-one in group or offset handling would corrupt later vectors, especially at metadata-group boundaries (offset not aligned to 2048) and in DELTA_FOR. It only runs when StandardColumnData::Select sees a full-vector scan and a validity select exists.

title: Hash join prefetch distance tuning (16 -> 32) plus prefetch on the probe-retry path
hypothesis: E0004 (software-pipelined prefetch at distance 16, 4MB gate) gave q09 -10..-15%, but the distance was never tuned. The profile still shows the o_orderkey = l_orderkey HASH_JOIN at 1.31s, the largest operator: 15M probe rows against a 3.27M-row build with a 64MB entry table, about 80% misses, so each probe is a DRAM miss. One loop iteration in ProbeForPointersInternal (join_hashtable.cpp:215) costs only a few ns on a miss (empty slot or salt mismatch, then break), so 16 iterations ahead (~50ns) is shorter than DRAM latency (~80-100ns plus TLB miss on a 64MB table). Many prefetches therefore arrive late. A distance of 32 should cover the latency and stay within the line-fill-buffer budget, because the loop issues one prefetch per iteration. The same applies to the build insert loop (InsertHashesLoop, line ~694), which writes into the same 64MB table.
plan: In src/execution/join_hashtable.cpp: change `HT_PREFETCH_DISTANCE` (line 200) from 16 to 32. That constant is used by both ProbeForPointersInternal (line 216) and InsertHashesLoop (line 694). Benchmark q09 at 16, 32 and 48, comparing back to back against the current best, and keep the best. If the time allows, try separate distances for probe and build. Leave the ShouldPrefetch gate (4MB) and everything else alone. Prefetch is only a hint, so results cannot change.
expected_gain: q09: 3-8% (the orders join probe and build, ~1.3s of operator time out of 0.78s total wall with 8 threads).
generality: Any hash join whose entry table is over 4MB (large builds, high-miss probes), e.g. fact-to-fact and fact-to-large-dimension joins in TPC-H/TPC-DS. Small joins are unaffected because of the gate. When a prefetch is wasted (count < distance), only the tail of the vector skips prefetching, so there is little downside.
risk: Low: one constant, no logic change. The main risk is the gain staying within noise.
